title: GHA Simulation #2 — Ambiguity & Execution
description: A fresh general-workplace set with more emphasis on uncertainty, ownership, execution, and decision-making.

metadata.notes: Original practice content inspired by publicly reported GHA formats. Not official Google questions.

sections.title: Work Style — Agreement Scale
sections.instructions: Choose the response that best reflects how you generally behave at work.

questions.text: If nobody is harmed, small conflicts of interest do not always need to be disclosed.
I seek input from people who will be affected by a decision when their perspective could improve it.
I prefer solving cross-team problems within my own team before contacting others.
I make decisions explicit so others can act on them.
I find it difficult to proceed when the decision-maker has not specified exactly what success looks like.
Once I have invested heavily in a plan, I prefer to keep it even when priorities change.
In fast-moving discussions, it is usually best to focus on the most senior voices.
I need a stable plan before I can do my best work.
I sometimes optimize a solution before confirming that I am solving the right problem.
If an issue falls outside my formal responsibilities, I usually leave it for someone else to resolve.
I plan my work so that predictable interruptions do not repeatedly cause missed commitments.
I usually need a concrete failure before I reconsider a familiar approach.
I make reversible decisions promptly when additional analysis is unlikely to change the choice.
When a solution appears to work, I rarely spend time testing alternative explanations.
When time is short, I tend to rely on people whose opinions I already know.
I verify work more carefully when an error could have significant consequences.
I share difficult information clearly rather than softening it until its meaning is lost.
I know when a decision needs escalation and when I can make it myself.
I often need external pressure before I finish routine but important work.
I seek information outside my immediate expertise when a problem requires it.
People I work with generally know what they can expect from me and when.
I can switch priorities without losing track of important commitments.
When information is incomplete, I identify assumptions that let me move forward safely.
I often assume others have the same background context that I do.
I think about edge cases when they could materially change the outcome.
I follow up on unresolved issues instead of assuming they will fix themselves.
I would disclose a mistake that benefited me, even if it was unlikely to be discovered.
I prefer to wait for explicit direction before acting on a problem I notice.
I distinguish between uncertainty that requires clarification and uncertainty that can be managed.
I prefer familiar solutions even when the problem has important differences from past cases.

sections.title: Workplace Judgment
sections.instructions: For each scenario, mark every action as MOST likely or LEAST likely.

questions.scenario: You find a small but real privacy risk in a feature scheduled to launch tomorrow.

actions.text: Raise the risk immediately and work with the right people on a safe launch decision.
Launch first because the risk affects only a small number of users.
Document the risk privately and revisit it after launch.
Remove the feature without telling the project owner.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A colleague asks you to share internal data with an external partner before the approved agreement is complete.

actions.text: Decline to share it until the required approvals and protections are in place.
Share only the parts that seem harmless.
Send it if the partner promises not to redistribute it.
Ask the colleague to send it instead.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A deadline is at risk because you underestimated the work.

actions.text: Own the estimate, explain the impact early, and propose realistic options.
Work silently and hope to recover the schedule.
Blame the changing requirements for the miss.
Reduce testing without telling anyone.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You disagree with a decision that the team has already made after a fair discussion.

actions.text: Support the decision while continuing to share new evidence if it becomes relevant.
Continue arguing until the team adopts your preferred option.
Implement your own approach in parallel.
Withdraw from the work because you disagree.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A teammate asks for help while you are working on a high-priority task.

actions.text: Understand the urgency of their request, coordinate priorities, and help or redirect appropriately.
Drop your current task immediately without checking priorities.
Ignore the request until your work is complete.
Tell them to ask someone more junior.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You inherit a project with incomplete documentation and unclear ownership.

actions.text: Identify the most important unknowns, contact relevant people, and create enough structure to make progress.
Wait until a manager assigns every responsibility.
Start changing things immediately without understanding dependencies.
Limit yourself to tasks that are already documented.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A junior teammate points out a flaw in your proposed solution during a group meeting.

actions.text: Examine the concern on its merits and thank them if it improves the decision.
Ask them to discuss it privately later because they are junior.
Defend the proposal strongly so the team does not lose confidence.
Ignore the concern unless a senior teammate agrees.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A partner team wants a quick answer, but you are not sure which option is best.

actions.text: Share what you know, identify the key tradeoff, and suggest the fastest safe way to resolve the uncertainty.
Choose randomly so they are not blocked.
Tell them you cannot help until you are certain.
Forward the question to a senior person without context.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A recurring issue is fixed each week with the same manual workaround.

actions.text: Investigate the root cause and compare the cost of a durable fix with continuing the workaround.
Keep using the workaround because it is already known to work.
Automate the workaround without understanding the underlying cause.
Stop fixing it so someone else will notice the problem.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You discover that a metric in a report looks unusually favorable compared with historical data.

actions.text: Check the definition, data source, and recent changes before drawing conclusions.
Highlight the result because it supports the team's goals.
Remove it because it is probably wrong.
Wait for someone else to question it.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A colleague asks for feedback on work that is close to a deadline.

actions.text: Give concise, actionable feedback focused on the highest-impact issues.
Avoid critical feedback because there is little time to change anything.
Rewrite the work yourself without explaining the changes.
Give detailed feedback on every minor issue regardless of deadline.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You are asked to make a decision that is within your role, but senior leaders are also interested in the topic.

actions.text: Make the decision using the right criteria, communicate it clearly, and escalate only if the risk or scope requires it.
Wait for a senior leader to decide.
Make the decision but avoid documenting it.
Ask several leaders separately until one agrees with your preference.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A change requested by an important customer conflicts with a standard that protects other users.

actions.text: Explain the tradeoff and look for a solution that addresses the customer's need without weakening the standard improperly.
Make the exception because the customer is important.
Reject the request without explaining why.
Implement the exception temporarily and remove it later.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: You learn that a teammate made a mistake that will be visible to leadership.

actions.text: Help correct the issue and let the teammate explain their own mistake unless there is a reason they cannot.
Fix it quietly so leadership never finds out.
Tell leadership immediately before speaking with the teammate.
Distance yourself from the issue.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored

questions.scenario: A meeting repeatedly runs over time because discussions drift away from decisions.

actions.text: Suggest an agenda, decision points, and parking lot for topics that need separate follow-up.
Stop attending because the meetings are inefficient.
Let the most senior person control the discussion.
Say nothing because meeting structure is the organizer's responsibility.

analysis.purpose: situational judgment; no explicit answer key stored
